analysis.one_liner: Restarts the clock for challenging pay discrimination each time a discriminatory paycheck is issued.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-199 in July 2007, but Senate Republicans blocked it from reaching a floor vote in April 2008 when a procedural motion failed 56-42, short of the 60 needed.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2007 the Supreme Court ruled in Ledbetter v. Goodyear that workers must file a pay discrimination claim within 180 days of the pay decision being made, even if they only learn of the discrimination years later. This bill would overturn that ruling under federal civil rights, age, and disability employment laws, by saying a discriminatory pay decision is legally 'occurring' each time a discriminatory paycheck or benefit is issued, including each new paycheck that carries forward the old disparity. Workers could also recover up to two years of back pay tied to related discrimination outside the usual filing window. It would apply retroactively to claims pending on or after May 28, 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid less because of their sex, race, religion, national origin, age, or disability, especially those who discover the disparity years after the initial decision, when the usual 180-day window has already closed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who discover pay discrimination late

how_it_helps.text: Declares that a discriminatory pay practice occurs each time wages, benefits, or other compensation is paid, so a worker can sue each time a discriminatory paycheck arrives rather than only within 180 days of the original decision.
Allows back pay recovery of up to two years before the filing of the charge when related discriminatory practices occurred outside the usual filing window.

Applies the fix to the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Rehabilitation Act, and applies it to pending claims as of May 28, 2007.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who carry forward discriminatory pay disparities face liability that accrues with each paycheck and possible back pay recovery of up to two years, with no fixed end point while the discriminatory pay practice continues.

drawbacks.text: Because liability keeps accruing with every paycheck, employers argue there is no fixed end to their exposure, which raises litigation risk and could push companies toward defensive pay documentation or settlement practices.

The bill applies retroactively to pending claims from May 28, 2007 forward, including conduct from before enactment, which employers and courts treating the Supreme Court ruling as final would contest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill fixes a real gap: pay discrimination is often hidden, and the Supreme Court's timing rule meant most victims could never sue because the 180-day window closed before they learned of the disparity. The cost is borne by employers, who face extended and effectively open-ended liability while a discriminatory pay practice continues, plus possible retroactive back pay. The two-year back pay cap does put some limit on how far back recovery reaches.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House, but in the Senate a motion to cut off debate so the bill could even be taken up failed 56-42, well short of the 60 needed, so the Senate never voted on the bill itself before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill responded to the Supreme Court's May 29, 2007 decision in Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., which Congress stated 'unduly restrict[ed] the time period in which victims of discrimination can challenge and recover for discriminatory compensation decisions.'
The House Committee on Education and Labor approved the bill 25-20 on June 27, 2007, and reported it amended on July 18.
The House passed the bill 225-199 on July 31, 2007, with Democrats voting 223-6 for it and Republicans voting 2-193 against.

The Senate took it up in April 2008, and a cloture motion to proceed failed 56-42 on April 23, 2008, short of the 60 votes needed to end debate, with Democrats voting 48-1 for and Republicans 6-41 against.
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on the measure on September 23, 2008, but the Senate never voted on the bill itself in the 110th Congress.
A successor version of the bill was enacted as law in January 2009 in the next Congress, becoming the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing pay discrimination claims, which escaped the extended liability for at least the remainder of that Congress; women and other workers paid unequally had to wait until the 2009 version became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared extended liability, until the 2009 law

for.name: George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative, chair of the House Education and Labor Committee, sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and his committee marked it up and reported it to the House floor within a month of introduction.

for.name: 223 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for the bill on passage, providing nearly all of its 225 votes.

for.name: 48 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted to end debate on the motion to proceed so the bill could be considered.

against.name: 41 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the motion to end debate, keeping the bill from reaching an up-or-down vote; it failed 56-42 with 60 needed.

against.name: 193 of 202 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the bill on passage.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: the House vote was 223-6 among Democrats versus 2-193 among Republicans, and in the Senate 48-1 among Democrats versus 6-41 among Republicans on the cloture vote.

industries.note: The bill would make each discriminatory paycheck a fresh legal violation, exposing employers to suits from workers who learned of pay disparities years after the initial decision, plus up to two years of back pay. That cost is the workers' gain; the Supreme Court ruling the bill overturned had the opposite effect.

industries.industry: Defense and civil rights employment-law bar
industries.note: A longer liability window creates more viable claims for workers and more work for plaintiffs' attorneys handling discrimination cases. This is a secondary effect of restoring workers' access to the courts.
